title: One word of peace (100–102)
hookLine: better than a thousand empty words is one word that brings peace
last: CALM THOUGHT — CALM THOUGHT, CALM WORD.

cards: How many words went through your day yesterday? Emails, texts, meetings, podcasts, a thread of three hundred comments, a group chat that never stops. Tens of thousands, easily.
Now try to remember one that actually helped: that settled you, or showed you something true, or made you kinder. Maybe you can find one. Maybe you can't.
The eighth chapter of the Dhammapada is built on that arithmetic: thousands against one.

teach.b: Verse one hundred, in Müller's English: “Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet.”

teach.h: THE TEST: DOES IT BRING QUIET?
teach.b: The test of a word isn't how impressive it is, or how many came with it. It's whether the person who hears it becomes quiet: settled, at peace.

Verses one hundred one and one hundred two say it twice more: a thousand verses of empty words, or a hundred, can't match one verse that brings peace. The commentary ties verse one hundred one to a striking story.

A man named Bahiya survived a shipwreck, came ashore wearing nothing but bark, and people began to treat him as a holy man. Troubled, he set out to find the Buddha, and found him on his alms round in the street.
Bahiya begged to be taught right there. Twice the Buddha said it wasn't the time.

teach.h: IN THE SEEN, ONLY THE SEEN.
teach.b: The third time, he gave him a teaching of just a few lines, roughly: in the seen, let there be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard. No extra story laid on top. Bahiya understood, the story says, on the spot.
A handful of words was all he needed. The chapter isn't against talking, or reading, or long teachings; you and i are reading a whole book together.
But among all the words, look for the one that calms. And when you're the one speaking, try to be that word.

how: Buddhist teachers often stress brief, well-chosen teaching, and the story of Bahiya, awakened by a teaching of a few lines, is widely told as an example.

o: the sound of many voices chanting at once
a thousand, as in a thousand empty words
a single verse that brings someone peace

games.q: match the pieces of verses one hundred to one hundred two.
p: worth less than one word of sense
taught in the street, on alms round

s: chapter eight says long teachings and reading are worthless
it says look for the word that brings peace; the reading itself goes on.
in the story, Bahiya asked three times before the Buddha taught him
then a teaching of just a few lines was enough.
verse one hundred measures a word by whether the hearer becomes quiet
not by how many words come with it.

games.q: you're the Buddha on your alms round. a stranger in bark clothes begs you to teach him right now, in the street. what do you do?
o: give a long discourse right there.
after he asks a third time, give him a few lines.
tell him to come to the monastery next week.
games.why: twice he said it wasn't the time; the third time he taught Bahiya a few lines: in the seen, only the seen. Bahiya understood on the spot.

practice: Let the noise of the day's words drift away, and try Bahiya's teaching: as you hear a sound, let it be only the sound, with no name for it and no story about it; as you feel the breath, only the feeling.
Then think of one person you'll talk to today, and let one simple sentence form that's true and useful, and might leave them a little calmer.

wordCard.voice: Sahassa. A thousand: better than a thousand empty words is a single word that, when someone hears it, brings them quiet.

orig.note: Pali: a thousand, the title of chapter eight (Sahassa Vagga).

carryVoice: Your line: one word that calms. In the seen, only the seen. That's day one hundred seventy-eight.

sources.q: Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet.

sources.ref: Udana 1.10 (Bahiya Sutta); Dhammapada-atthakatha, story of Bahiya Daruciriya (verse 101)
